Extreme Heat

riskFindings:
Extreme Heat
Ahmedabad runs high risk of extreme heat events; temperatures rising at 0.15°C/decade (1970-2020). Heat wave events increased by 4 events (1951-2019) and projected to increase by 5-30 events by 2070. Land surface temperature varies between 29°C to 47°C. Vulnerable areas include Amraiwadi, Bapunagar, Viratnagar and industrial zones.

Urban Flooding
4.3% of city area affected by urban flooding/waterlogging, impacting ~9.5% of population (~0.7 million people). Vulnerable areas include Naranpura, Khokhra, Bodakdev, Paldi, Maninagar, Vasna and Vatva. Residents within 250m of 166 waterlogged/flood points face elevated risk.

Air Pollution
Ahmedabad is listed as a non-attainment city by CPCB. Key pollutants are PM10 and PM2.5. Road dust, domestic sector, construction and point sources (industries) are major contributors.

riskFindings:
Urban Flooding
Total area of ~180 sq. km in the city is at risk of floods, hosting ~21% of population. Flood risk categorised into High (6% of population), Medium (4%) and Low (11%) risk zones. Peripheral zones — Yelahanka (North), Mahadevapura (East), RR Nagar (Southwest) — are highest priority areas.

Urban Heat
Mean air temperature rising at 0.23°C/decade since 1975; increase accelerated to ~0.5°C/decade in last decade. Number of heat wave incidents peaking; since 1975, city faces ~1.5 additional 'caution' days of high heat index every two years. Areas such as Peenya, Hebbal and Nagarabhavi show higher land surface temperatures (35–36°C).

Drought
84% of the Cauvery-Ponnaiyar Basin area is in the 'very high risk' category for drought. Region is 'overexploited' for groundwater. Since 2000, a further 31% of city area has seen decline in groundwater recharge potential.

Thunderstorms & Lightning
City gets ~44 days of thunderstorms per year on average. Karnataka saw a 68.74% rise in lightning strikes in 2021-22.

Air Pollution
Annual PM10 averages vary between 60-123 µg/m³. PM2.5 bordering CPCB limits at 30-40 µg/m³ per year.

strategies.strategy:
1) 40% of new appliance technology will be of high-range energy efficiency, 42% of new residential buildings and 48% of new commercial buildings will adopt insulated walls and roofs, improved window technology, and improved building services design, 100% transition from solid fuel to clean cooking fuel  by 2030;  
2) 92% of the new households in the city (from 2019) should be in Transit-Oriented Development areas by 2050. The combined share of public transport (PT) and non-motorised transport (NMT) in total no. of trips to be 75% by 2030, 80% by 2040, 85% by 2050.  90% of cars and motorcycles, 75% of buses to be powered by cleaner fuels by 2050. 47% of total freight vehicles to be powered by cleaner fuels by 2050.;
3)  Achieve 100% segregation of waste by 2025 and achieve over 90% diversion of waste from landfills by 2050 (60% by 2030 & 75% by 2040). Recycling of paper & plastic waste to be >60% by 2030, >75% by 2040 & >90% by 2050.   Achieve about 25% gas capture from scientific landfill by 2030, 50% by 2040 & 75% by 2050. 
4)  To achieve 40% reduction in PM10 concentration and 30% reduction in PM2.5 concentration by 2026 from 2017-18 levels as per revised targets prescribed by NCAP.  30% of commercial and institutional buildings complying with WHO Indoor air quality standards and guidelines by 2030. Preparation of a roadmap for a comprehensive health action plan tackling risks due to air pollution for 2025-2035. To procure 13 new CAAQMS and transition the existing manual station to CAAQMS systems by 2035. 
5)  100% households to have access to water and sanitation infrastructure and services, which are a combination of networked and decentralised systems.  By 2050, aim to reduce non-revenue water to 15%. Achieve reuse of treated wastewater to a minimum of 50% by 2030 and 90% by 2050. 40% of city's surface area to become permeable by 2040 by reclaiming ecologically sensitive spaces and adopting nature-based solutions. Convert 75% of the city's footpaths to permeable surface material by 2050.  95% wastewater treatment with a combination of centralised and decentralised system with about 61% low-carbon wastewater treatment technologies by 2050 . 
6) Prepare and adopt the RMP 2041 and set up the Master Plan Coordination Committee by 2025. All spatial plans and DCRs to adopt climate action as a lens by 2030.  Conserve and restore all blue-green networks in the city. All urban infrastructure schemes and projects should adhere to disaster resilience standards. Increase the city's tree cover (canopy) from the baseline by 10% by 2030 and 20% by 2040. Increase the city's green (vegetation) cover and permeable surfaces to 40% of the city's area by 2040, to tackle flood- and heat-related disaster risk reduction. Convert 75% of the city's footpaths to permeable surface material by 2050. Operationalise the (recently re-constituted) BMC by 2023 and prepare the People's Biodiversity Register by 2025. By 2050, provide safe and affordable housing for 100% urban poor and vulnerable groups in locations having access to public transport stops/stations within a 5-minute walk. By 2050, increase the city's publicly accessible per capita open space from the existing 2.2 sq. m to 6 sq. m 
7) A comprehensive and regularly updated data repository for the city. A comprehensive disaster management plan.  Empowered ward committees for better localised preparedness for, response to, and recovery from disasters. Reduction in loss of life, livelihoods, and assets due to climate and environmental hazards..

Urban Flooding

riskFindings:
Urban Flooding
Composite flood risk mapping identifies 9% of city area at high risk (Ward 10 and near Railway Station in Ward 1), 18% at moderate risk (Wards 4, 9, 12) and 73% at low risk. City's low elevation (20m MSL) and erratic rainfall makes it highly flood-prone. River dam overflow contributed to 2021 flash floods.

Cyclone / Storm Surge Risk
Coastal location makes Jamnagar highly vulnerable; over 120 cyclones from the Arabian Sea have impacted the Gujarat coastal region in the past century. Wind speeds can exceed 55 m/sec (almost 200 km/h). Storm surges cause saline water intrusion rendering fertile land unproductive.

Seismic Vulnerability
Jamnagar falls under Zone-IV (0.24g) of seismic vulnerability, translating to moderate risk of earthquakes with shaking intensity 2.3× the Design Basis Earthquake standard.

Drought / Water Scarcity
SPEI data reveals 3 severe drought events since 1951. Minimum temperature rise of 0.1–1.5°C observed; frequency of hot days increasing to 30 and hot nights to 24. Saltwater intrusion in estuaries due to reduced freshwater flows is increasing.

riskFindings:
Urban Heat
City experiencing higher temperatures and variable heat stress driven by urban heat island (UHI) effects. Areas with dense informal settlements and limited green cover are most exposed.

Urban Flooding
Flood-prone areas routinely waterlogged during monsoons and submerged for several hours during extreme rainfall events (EREs). By 2080, likelihood of urban floods like the 2005 event is projected to more than double. 2005 deluge caused financial losses estimated at USD 1,100 million, of which ~USD 245 million borne by marginalised population. By 2070s, Mumbai projected to be among the top Asian cities in population exposed to coastal flooding.

Landslides
Landslide-prone areas experience heavy loss and damages during EREs, especially where retaining walls are weak.

Coastal Risks
Upward trend of cyclonic events in the Arabian Sea due to warming seas increasing coastal risks. Coastal communities face inundation during non-monsoon days from high tides. Sea level rise projections compound this risk.

Air Pollution
Increasing traffic congestion, unregulated construction, and mismanaged solid waste elevate air pollution risks and health impacts, particularly for vulnerable communities.

Heat Waves
Nagpur has witnessed extreme temperatures for 21 days (double the typical heat wave duration) in 2013. Temperatures have exceeded 45°C for seven consecutive summers. In the last 10 years, 196 cases of sunstroke were recorded and 18 resulted in deaths. Annual average temperature shows upward trend since 1981.

Urban Flooding
In 2018, Nagpur recorded 265mm of rainfall in just 9 hours, causing widespread flooding, loss of lives and property damage. Record highest 24-hr rainfall is 304 mm (July 12, 1994). Overall drainage coverage remains poor and inadequate despite regular cleaning.

Drought / Water Scarcity
Nagpur witnessed 12 incidents of droughts between 1901 and 1998 (per IMD). Annual average precipitation shows a decreasing trend (1989-2018).

Hailstorms
Nagpur district witnessed the highest number of hailstorm events (40) in India in the last 38 years (1972–2011), though frequency within the urban area is very low.

riskFindings:
Extreme Heat
Over half (57%) of the city area is designated as heat hotspots, with Land Surface Temperature (LST) exceeding the median of 37°C. This directly impacts 64% of the population (~356,016 people as of 2021). Temperatures in hotspot areas reach 42°C to 43°C. Key hotspot areas include Madri industrial area, MLSU and other educational institutions, RHB colonies in Hiran Magri, and congested residential developments on hillocks. Additionally, 76% of street vendors (2,117 people) and 29% of population (young children and elderly) are particularly vulnerable.

Urban Flooding
Udaipur's saucer-like topography creates a natural basin for water accumulation. 50 locations identified as prone to waterlogging during rainy season, especially near the Ayad River and city centre. Urban flooding affects ~13% of the city's total area, impacting 17% of the population. 5,537 slum dwellers (35% of total slum population) and 1,407 street vendors (51% of total) face heightened flood risks.

riskFindings:
Floods
On July 26, 2005, suburban Mumbai and Thane experienced one of the worst floods in their history and received the highest ever rainfall recorded in the last 100 years in India.




Landslides
With the pressure on land, many vacant sites on hill slopes or bottoms of hills have turned into inhabited area and thereby become vulnerable to landslides. Most cases of landslides occur during heavy rain associated with high velocity winds. It sometimes results in loss of human lives and damages to structures.




Cyclones
Due to the close proximity to the sea and presence of hilly region on one side, the coastal wards of Thane (facing the Arabian Sea) are prone to gusty winds and cyclonic impacts.




Earthquakes
Though earthquakes are not considered as climate event but Thane must prepare for them. . As per the Vulnerability Atlas of India – 2nd Edition, BMTPC, Thane district lies in earthquake hazard zone III.14 In the years 1983, 1984 and 1985, Khardi taluka in Thane district received earthquake shocks.

sectorContribution: 2015–2020: Industry/Transport/Energy 109.77 Mt; Agriculture 25.07 Mt; Waste 0.66 Mt; LULUCF -36.9 Mt; subtotal 135.49 Mt
climateRisks: Cyclones; sea-level rise; coastal inundation; heatwaves; floods; drought/water stress; vector- and water-borne disease
riskFindings: 480 km coastline is cyclone-exposed; several coastal ecosystems face permanent-inundation risk by 2050; 30–40% of districts experience >45°C temperatures during March–June; all districts are heat-stress-prone.

strategies.sector: 12 sectors including NAPCC missions plus state-led Health and Coastal & Disaster Risk Management.
strategies.strategy: Combine climate-resilient infrastructure and ecosystems with low-carbon energy, industry, transport and resource management.
strategies.action: Strengthen cyclone/flood preparedness; climate-smart agriculture; water security; coastal ecosystem restoration; heat-health action; renewable energy and efficiency.
strategies.intervention: Early warning and cyclone shelters; resilient agriculture; coastal/mangrove restoration; water conservation; renewable energy; efficient industry/transport; heat-health systems.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile reports the 2012 sectoral emissions figures and per-capita emissions; net total above is a derived value, not a directly quoted SAPCC total. | Official MoEFCC SAPCC profile and Odisha SAPCC report provide sectoral and net totals.

vision: Climate-resilient and sustainable development that protects agriculture, water, ecosystems and vulnerable communities.
goals: Reduce heat and water stress; strengthen climate-resilient agriculture and groundwater management; improve energy efficiency and clean energy; strengthen health and ecosystem resilience.
organizations: Directorate of Environment & Climate Change; Punjab State Council for Science & Technology; State Climate Change Knowledge Centre; line departments.
sectorContribution: Agriculture; Water; Forests; Energy; Industry; Transport; Health
climateRisks: Extreme heat; drought/water stress; changing rainfall; agricultural risks; air pollution/health
riskFindings: Days above 40°C have increased substantially; rainfall shows a declining historical trend; future warming is projected across the state, with strong implications for agriculture and water.

strategies.sector: Seven State Missions aligned with NAPCC.
strategies.strategy: Shift Punjab toward climate-resilient agriculture and water management while reducing energy and emissions intensity.
strategies.action: Promote crop diversification and water-efficient agriculture; conserve groundwater; expand renewable energy and efficiency; strengthen heat-health and ecosystem management.
strategies.intervention: Micro-irrigation; crop diversification; groundwater recharge; solar/renewable energy; energy-efficient pumps; heat-health preparedness; afforestation.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile reports SAPCC 2.0 for 2021–2030 and district-level vulnerability assessment.

vision: Sustainable development with climate resilience in an arid and water-stressed state.
goals: Reduce vulnerability to water scarcity, drought and heat; strengthen agriculture, livestock and desert ecosystems; improve energy efficiency and renewable energy; mainstream climate resilience.
organizations: Department of Environment & Forests; TERI; GIZ; state line departments.
sectorContribution: 1990: CO2 18.6 Mt, CH4 827.9 kt, N2O 6.6 kt; 1995: CO2 27.0 Mt, CH4 1,044 kt, N2O 10.5 kt. Revised SAPCC uses 2018–19 as base year for emissions profiling.
climateRisks: Drought; extreme heat; water scarcity; rainfall variability; desertification; ecosystem and livestock stress
riskFindings: Arid climate and water scarcity make agriculture, livestock and ecosystems highly climate-sensitive; long-term resilience depends on water security and sustainable land management.

strategies.sector: Seven priority sectors in the original RAPCC.
strategies.strategy: Improve water and livelihood security while promoting sustainable land, energy and ecosystem management.
strategies.action: Water conservation and efficiency; drought-resilient agriculture; livestock adaptation; renewable energy; ecosystem restoration; resilient health/disaster systems.
strategies.intervention: Rainwater harvesting; watershed development; drought-resilient crops; efficient irrigation; solar energy; rangeland/desert ecosystem management.
strategies.info: MoEFCC identifies the RAPCC v1.0 as released 4 September 2014; a revised plan should be substituted once formally approved/listed. | Official Rajasthan SAPCC 1.0 reports 1990/1995 totals; revised 2022 SAPCC states 2018–19 is the base year for historical emission profiling.

vision: Climate-resilient sustainable development that protects the fragile Himalayan environment and ecosystem services.
goals: Strengthen water and agriculture resilience; improve energy efficiency; protect forests and biodiversity; climate-proof rural and urban habitats.
organizations: Department of Science & Technology; High Level Coordination Committee; GIZ; state departments.
sectorContribution: Water; Agriculture & Horticulture; Energy Efficiency; Urban & Rural Habitats; Forests & Biodiversity
climateRisks: Temperature rise; shifting rainfall; glacier/water-system sensitivity; landslides; biodiversity and ecosystem stress
riskFindings: The steep Himalayan terrain and changing temperature/rainfall patterns create risks for water, agriculture, forests, settlements and infrastructure.

strategies.sector: Five working groups/sectors in SAPCC v1.0.
strategies.strategy: Protect Himalayan ecosystems and strengthen climate resilience of water, agriculture, energy and habitats.
strategies.action: Improve watershed and spring management; climate-resilient agriculture/horticulture; energy efficiency; forest and biodiversity conservation; resilient settlements.
strategies.intervention: Spring/watershed restoration; resilient crops; energy efficiency; forest conservation; slope/landslide management; resilient rural/urban infrastructure.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile notes increasing temperatures and shifting seasonal rainfall across 2030s, 2050s and 2080s projections.

vision: Climate-resilient development under Vision 2023, with sustainable agriculture, water, ecosystems, energy and habitats.
goals: Strengthen coastal and water resilience; promote sustainable agriculture and biodiversity; expand renewable energy and energy efficiency; improve sustainable habitat and climate knowledge.
organizations: Department of Environment, Government of Tamil Nadu; State Climate Change Cell; state departments; technical partners.
sectorContribution: Power sector contributes 67%
climateRisks: Cyclones; sea-level rise; coastal flooding/salinity; extreme rainfall; heat; drought/water stress
riskFindings: Long coastline is exposed to cyclones, sea-level rise and salinity; climate projections indicate rising temperatures, changing monsoon patterns and more extreme rainfall.

strategies.sector: Seven focus areas in the SAPCC framework; revised SAPCC 2.0 is associated with the 2020–2030 period.
strategies.strategy: Integrate climate resilience and low-carbon development across water, agriculture, coasts, energy, habitats and knowledge systems.
strategies.action: Strengthen coastal protection; water conservation; climate-resilient agriculture; forest/biodiversity conservation; renewable energy and efficiency; sustainable habitat and knowledge systems.
strategies.intervention: Coastal/mangrove restoration; rainwater harvesting; resilient crops; renewable energy; efficient buildings; sustainable urban planning; climate information systems.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile records the original plan's seven focus areas; revised-plan status should be read alongside the current Tamil Nadu Climate Change Mission materials. | Tamil Nadu Climate Change Mission material cited by UN-Habitat reports 173 MtCO2e and 67% power-sector contribution for the state.

vision: Climate-resilient development suited to a semi-arid state, integrating adaptation with sustainable economic development.
goals: Reduce drought and heat vulnerability; strengthen water, agriculture and forests; improve urban and infrastructure resilience; promote clean energy and climate knowledge.
organizations: Environment Protection Training & Research Institute (EPTRI); Department of Environment, Forests, Science & Technology; state line departments.
sectorContribution: Agriculture & Allied; Forestry & Biodiversity; Energy; Industries/Mining; Transport; Health; Urban Development; Tourism; Rural Development; Climate Research
climateRisks: Drought; heatwaves; floods; changing monsoon; groundwater stress; vector- and water-borne disease
riskFindings: Telangana is semi-arid with recurring drought and heatwaves; Hyderabad has experienced urban flooding; groundwater-dependent agriculture is vulnerable to declining water tables.

strategies.sector: Ten sectors identified in the original SAPCC.
strategies.strategy: Strengthen water and agricultural resilience while improving urban systems, ecosystems, health and low-carbon energy.
strategies.action: Restore tanks and watersheds; climate-resilient agriculture; expand renewable energy and efficiency; improve urban drainage; protect forests; strengthen health and research.
strategies.intervention: Mission Kakatiya/tank restoration; micro-irrigation; drought/flood-resilient crops; Haritha Haram/afforestation; LED/energy efficiency; urban drainage and heat action.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile confirms the plan was prepared after Telangana's 2014 bifurcation and lists ten sectors.

vision: Climate-resilient and low-carbon development aligned with NDCs and SDGs.
goals: Reduce vulnerability of agriculture, forests, water, health and settlements; improve renewable energy and efficiency; strengthen ecosystem and disaster resilience.
organizations: State climate-change institutional framework; Department of Forest/Environment; line departments; technical partners.
sectorContribution: Agriculture; Forests & Biodiversity; Water; Energy; Sustainable Habitat; Health; Strategic Knowledge; Disaster Management
climateRisks: Extreme rainfall/floods; drought; heat; forest and biodiversity stress; agriculture and livelihood risks
riskFindings: SAPCC 2.0 uses IPCC AR5 vulnerability methodology and prioritises adaptation and mitigation across eight state sectors/missions.

strategies.sector: 83 prioritised actions: 44 adaptation, 34 mitigation and 5 both.
strategies.strategy: Integrate climate resilience and emissions reduction into state development and sectoral programmes.
strategies.action: Climate-resilient agriculture; water conservation; forest/biodiversity protection; clean energy; resilient habitat; climate-health and disaster preparedness.
strategies.intervention: Agroforestry; watershed management; renewable energy; energy efficiency; ecosystem restoration; resilient infrastructure and early warning.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile records SAPCC 2.0 for 2021–2030 and the 83-action portfolio.

vision: Climate-resilient, sustainable and low-carbon development aligned with national missions, NDCs and SDGs.
goals: Reduce vulnerability to heat, floods, drought and water stress; strengthen agriculture, forests and health; improve energy, transport and urban resilience; mainstream climate action.
organizations: Department of Environment, Forest & Climate Change; Directorate of Environment; state departments and technical partners.
sectorContribution: 2015: electricity generation 123.80 MtCO2e; residential 13.69; commercial 1.03; agriculture 4.93; transport 20.20
climateRisks: Heat; floods; drought; rainfall variability; water stress; air pollution/health; agricultural vulnerability
riskFindings: Projected warming is substantial; near-term rainfall is projected to decline under both RCPs; high dependence on the monsoon increases agriculture and water risks.

strategies.sector: Eight State Missions, 39 strategies and 179 actions; 29% mitigation, 59% adaptation and 12% both.
strategies.strategy: Combine large-scale adaptation with mitigation across energy, agriculture, water, transport, habitat and ecosystems.
strategies.action: Climate-resilient agriculture and water management; clean energy and efficiency; resilient urban/transport systems; ecosystem restoration; health and disaster preparedness.
strategies.intervention: Efficient irrigation; crop diversification; renewable energy; clean mobility; urban greening; watershed/river restoration; heat-health and disaster systems.
strategies.info: MoEFCC reports total SAPCC 2.0 budget of ₹1,12,204.79 crore, with a reported financing gap. | Government of Uttar Pradesh climate knowledge portal reproduces GHG Platform India estimates for 2005–2015.

vision: Climate-resilient development that protects Himalayan ecosystems, livelihoods and infrastructure.
goals: Reduce disaster and climate risk; strengthen agriculture, forests, water, livestock, health, energy and tourism resilience; climate-proof transport and urban development.
organizations: State Forest Department; State Council for Climate Change; 11 sectoral Working Groups; UNDP; state departments.
sectorContribution: Agriculture; Forests; Water Resources; Livestock & Animal Husbandry; Health; Industry; Disaster; Energy; Roads & Transport; Urban Development; Tourism
climateRisks: Glacier retreat; GLOFs; landslides; floods; cloudbursts; forest fires; warming; changing rainfall
riskFindings: The 2013 flood disaster is a major reference point; Himalayan projections indicate warming and rainfall changes, with potential increases in sediment yield and slope hazards.

strategies.sector: 11 sectoral Working Groups in the original UAPCC.
strategies.strategy: Build resilience of Himalayan ecosystems, livelihoods and infrastructure while strengthening disaster preparedness and sustainable development.
strategies.action: Strengthen spring/water systems; climate-resilient agriculture/livestock; forest and fire management; resilient roads/towns; disaster preparedness; sustainable tourism.
strategies.intervention: Spring/watershed restoration; resilient crops/livestock; forest restoration/fire control; resilient roads and settlements; early warning; climate-smart tourism.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile records the original UAPCC and its 11-sector structure; updated revision status should be checked when formally approved.

vision: Climate-resilient development protecting the Sundarbans, Himalayan ecosystems, agriculture and vulnerable livelihoods.
goals: Reduce risks from sea-level rise, cyclones, floods and extreme rainfall; protect Sundarbans and biodiversity; improve water, agriculture, health and resilient habitats.
organizations: Department of Environment & Climate Change, Government of West Bengal; state line departments; State Steering Committee.
sectorContribution: Agriculture; Water; Forests & Biodiversity; Sundarbans/Coastal; Habitat; Health; Energy; Transport; Industry; Strategic Knowledge
climateRisks: Sea-level rise; cyclones/storm surge; coastal flooding; river floods; extreme rainfall; drought; biodiversity stress
riskFindings: Sundarbans face sea-level-rise-driven inundation and cyclone risk; Darjeeling hills and Gangetic plains have distinct vulnerabilities; arsenic/fluoride contamination and climate-sensitive livelihoods add risk.

strategies.sector: About ten climate-sensitive sectors organised around NAPCC missions.
strategies.strategy: Protect coastal and Himalayan ecosystems and climate-sensitive livelihoods while strengthening resilient agriculture, water, health and habitats.
strategies.action: Sundarbans/mangrove protection; cyclone and flood resilience; climate-resilient agriculture; water security; biodiversity conservation; resilient health and housing.
strategies.intervention: Mangrove restoration; embankment/coastal protection; resilient agriculture; water-quality management; early warning and disaster shelters; ecosystem-based adaptation.
strategies.info: MoEFCC profile states the first part was submitted in April 2011 and the second version added Habitats, Sundarbans and Darjeeling Himalayas.
